name: find-tail
summary: The suffix of the list starting at the first element that satisfies the predicate, or #f if none does.
explanation: find answers WHAT matched. find-tail answers WHERE it matched, by handing back the rest of the list from that point on. The distinction matters for two reasons. First, it disambiguates: (find even? '(1 3 #f 4)) is 4, but (find even? '(1 #f 3)) is #f, and so is a search that failed -- you cannot tell a found #f from a missing one. find-tail never has that problem, because a successful search returns a pair and a failed one returns #f, and a pair is never #f. Second, the returned suffix is the ACTUAL tail, eq? to the corresponding cdr of the input, not a copy. That makes find-tail a cursor: you can find a marker in a list, then keep walking from there, or take everything before it by comparing lengths. It is the list-search verb that composes, and the one to reach for whenever the answer to 'is it in here' is going to be followed by 'and what comes after it'.

examples.note: (4 1 5) -- the search stops at 4 and hands back everything from there.
(found (4 1 5) element 4 missing #f) -- find gives the element, find-tail gives the position, and a failed search is plainly #f.

examples.code:
(define items '(intro body body marker tail tail))
(define after (find-tail (lambda (x) (eq? x 'marker)) items))
(display (list 'after after 'before (- (length items) (length after))))
(newline)
examples.note: (after (marker tail tail) before 3) -- because the answer is the real suffix, subtracting lengths recovers how many elements came before it.

caveats: It returns a PAIR, not the element. (car (find-tail pred xs)) is what find would have given you. Forgetting the car is the usual first mistake.
A failed search is #f, and #f is not a list. (length (find-tail even? '(1 3))) raises. Check the result before you walk it.
The suffix is SHARED with the input, not copied -- it is eq? to the matching cdr. Mutating it mutates the original list.
The predicate must accept one argument. find-tail passes elements one at a time; it is not the multi-list variant that map and for-each are.
On an empty list it answers #f without ever calling the predicate, which is right but means a predicate with a side effect will not fire.
usecases: Splitting a list at a marker: find-tail gives the second half, and the lengths give you the first.
Distinguishing 'found the value #f' from 'found nothing', which plain find cannot do.
Walking a stream of tokens to the next delimiter and carrying on from there.

learn.concept: Returning a position instead of a value is what turns a search into something you can keep searching from.
learn.progression: Use find first and be happy. Then search a list that contains #f, watch find lie to you, and reach for find-tail. Then notice the suffix is eq? to the original's cdr, and you have discovered why member exists rather than a boolean contains?.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define log '(boot boot warn warn error done))
(define (from-first-error entries)
  (let ((tail (find-tail (lambda (e) (eq? e 'error)) entries)))
    (if tail tail '())))
(display (list 'tail (from-first-error log)
               'clean (from-first-error '(boot done))
               'immediate (from-first-error '(error done))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (first-index-above bound xs)
  (let ((tail (find-tail (lambda (n) (> n bound)) xs)))
    (if tail (- (length xs) (length tail)) 'none)))
(display (map (lambda (b) (first-index-above b '(1 4 9 16 25)))
              '(0 5 20 99)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define holes '(1 #f 3))
(display (list 'find-says (find (lambda (x) (not x)) holes)
               'find-tail-says (find-tail (lambda (x) (not x)) holes)
               'find-on-miss (find (lambda (x) (eq? x 'zzz)) holes)
               'find-tail-on-miss (find-tail (lambda (x) (eq? x 'zzz)) holes)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: An operator has a log and wants everything from the first error onward. Candidates: find-tail (one pass, gives the suffix directly, and #f is unambiguous because the elements are symbols and a pair is never #f), find (gives only the symbol error back, which you already knew), member with eq? (works for this case, but only compares against a fixed value -- it cannot take a predicate), a hand-written named let (fine, and it is exactly what find-tail already is), filter (wrong shape entirely -- it keeps every error, not the tail from the first one). find-tail is the pick because the question is positional.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: slicing a log from its first error, with the clean case and the already-at-the-front case both shown. math: turning the suffix back into an index by subtracting lengths, across four thresholds including one nothing exceeds. cs: the disambiguation demonstrated directly -- find returns #f both when it finds #f and when it finds nothing, and find-tail tells the two apart.
row-2-audit.meta: Why find-tail and not member: member is the special case where the predicate is 'equal to this one value'. When the test is a computation rather than a comparison, find-tail is the general verb and member is the sugar.
row-2-audit.eng: Log slicing wants the position, not the value. Reaching for find and then re-scanning to locate it is two passes for a one-pass question.
row-2-audit.math: |xs| - |suffix| is the index of the first match. That identity only works because the suffix is a genuine tail and its length is measured against the same list.
row-2-audit.cs: A verb whose failure value can also be a success value is a verb you cannot compose safely. Returning a pair instead of an element is how SRFI-1 escapes that.

row-3-dimension.setup: Scanning forward until something is true, and keeping hold of where you stopped rather than what you saw.

rungs.domain: a strip of hourly rainfall readings in millimetres, looking for the onset of a storm
rungs.code:
(define hourly '(0 0 1 12 30 8 0))
(define (from-onset mm-per-hour threshold)
  (or (find-tail (lambda (mm) (>= mm threshold)) mm-per-hour) '()))
(display (list 'storm (from-onset hourly 10) 'drizzle (from-onset hourly 1) 'dry (from-onset hourly 99)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a tokenizer positioning itself at the next statement separator
rungs.code:
(define tokens '(let x = 1 |;| print x |;|))
(define (next-statement toks)
  (let ((tail (find-tail (lambda (t) (eq? t '|;|)) toks)))
    (if tail (cdr tail) '())))
(define (statement toks)
  (let ((tail (find-tail (lambda (t) (eq? t '|;|)) toks)))
    (if tail (- (length toks) (length tail)) (length toks))))
(display (list 'first-length (statement tokens) 'rest (next-statement tokens)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers it is a scan with three outcomes: a match in the middle, no match at all, and a match not at the head. On measured data it becomes onset detection -- the hour the rain crossed a threshold, with everything after it, which is the shape every 'when did this start' question has. In a tokenizer it becomes cursor arithmetic: the tail past the separator is the next statement, and the distance to the tail is the length of the current one, so one call answers both halves of the split. The verb is identical each time; what climbs is how much of the answer lives in the POSITION rather than the value.
row-3-dimension.meta: The rungs are distinguished by what the suffix is used for: printed, thresholded, and then differenced against the original to recover an index. Only the third rung actually needs the eq? sharing guarantee, and that is the rung where a copy would have been a silent performance bug.
row-3-dimension.eng: Onset detection is find-tail with a threshold predicate. Writing it as a loop with an index is the same computation with more places to be off by one.
row-3-dimension.math: Thresholding is a monotone predicate applied pointwise; the first crossing is well defined even though the series is not monotone.
row-3-dimension.cs: A parser that returns a suffix rather than an index never has to carry the original list alongside a cursor, which removes an entire class of desynchronisation bug.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (tail-is-real-tail? pred xs)
  (let ((t (find-tail pred xs)))
    (if t (equal? t (list-tail xs (- (length xs) (length t)))) #t)))
(display (map (lambda (xs) (tail-is-real-tail? even? xs))
              '((3 1 4 1 5) (2 4 6) (1 3 5) () (7 7 8))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (car-agrees-with-find? pred xs)
  (let ((t (find-tail pred xs)))
    (if t (equal? (car t) (find pred xs)) (not (find pred xs)))))
(display (map (lambda (xs) (car-agrees-with-find? (lambda (n) (> n 3)) xs))
              '((1 2 9 4) (9) (1 2) () (4 4 4))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (nothing-before-it? pred xs)
  (let ((t (find-tail pred xs)))
    (if t
        (let ((before (list-head xs (- (length xs) (length t)))))
          (not (find pred before)))
        (not (find pred xs)))))
(display (map (lambda (xs) (nothing-before-it? odd? xs))
              '((2 4 5 7) (1 2 3) (2 4 6) () (0 0 9 9))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: The result is always a genuine suffix of the input; its car is always exactly what find would have returned; and no element before it satisfies the predicate -- which is what makes it the FIRST match rather than any match.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all predicates p and lists xs, if find-tail(p, xs) = t then t = list-tail(xs, |xs| - |t|), car(t) = find(p, xs), and for all e in the prefix xs[0, |xs|-|t|). not p(e); and if find-tail(p, xs) = #f then find(p, xs) = #f
row-4-proof.meta: Three independent claims: that it is a suffix at all, that it agrees with find, and that it is the earliest such suffix. What would falsify them: a returned list that was equal? but positioned wrong, a car that disagreed with find on a list containing #f, or a match found late when an earlier one existed. The empty list appears in all three because it is where the loop is never entered, and the all-matching list appears because that is where the suffix is the whole input and the prefix is empty.
row-4-proof.eng: The suffix law is what licenses you to treat the result as a slice of the original rather than as new data that has to be reconciled.
row-4-proof.math: Firstness is a minimality claim, and minimality is proved by showing the excluded prefix is empty of matches -- not by showing the match exists.
row-4-proof.cs: The agreement with find is the compatibility contract. If it ever broke, every call site that had migrated from find to find-tail would silently change meaning.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (skip-to marker entries)
  (or (find-tail (lambda (e) (eq? e marker)) entries) '()))
(define (sections marker entries)
  (let loop ((rest entries) (out '()))
    (let ((tail (skip-to marker rest)))
      (if (null? tail)
          (reverse (if (null? rest) out (cons rest out)))
          (loop (cdr tail) (cons (list-head rest (- (length rest) (length tail))) out))))))
(display (sections 'break '(a b break c break d e)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (first-crossing bound xs)
  (find-tail (lambda (n) (>= n bound)) xs))
(define (crossing-index bound xs)
  (let ((t (first-crossing bound xs)))
    (if t (- (length xs) (length t)) -1)))
(define series '(1 1 2 3 5 8 13 21))
(display (map (lambda (b) (crossing-index b series)) '(1 3 10 100)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (cursor-at pred toks) (find-tail pred toks))
(define (count-runs pred toks)
  (let loop ((rest toks) (n 0))
    (let ((t (cursor-at pred rest)))
      (if t (loop (cdr t) (+ n 1)) n))))
(display (list 'semicolons (count-runs (lambda (t) (eq? t 'sep)) '(a sep b sep c))
               'none (count-runs (lambda (t) (eq? t 'sep)) '(a b))
               'only (count-runs (lambda (t) (eq? t 'sep)) '(sep sep sep))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: find-tail answers where the first match is, as the rest of the list from there.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: skip-to is one call; sections calls it in a loop, and because each answer is a real suffix the loop can measure the prefix and cut it off -- splitting a list on a delimiter falls out with no index arithmetic and no accumulator of elements. math: first-crossing is one call; crossing-index turns it into a number, and mapping THAT over a set of thresholds profiles a whole series in one line. cs: cursor-at is one call; count-runs steps past each match and counts, which is a scanner -- the same loop a lexer runs, with the predicate as the only parameter.
row-5-emergence.meta: Every composition here is the same move: call the helper, consume one element past its answer, recur. That works only because the answer is a position rather than a value -- with plain find, each of these three would need a second traversal to locate what it had already found.
row-5-emergence.eng: Splitting on a delimiter is the most-rewritten five lines in any codebase. Building it on a positional search makes it a fold instead of a state machine.
row-5-emergence.math: Mapping a crossing detector over a range of thresholds is a cheap way to summarise a monotone-ish series without sorting it.
row-5-emergence.cs: A scanner is a cursor plus a loop. Once the search verb returns cursors, the scanner is four lines and the predicate is the only thing that varies between one language's lexer and another's.
